It seems to me most important that the man at the head of the Royal Military College should be a man thoroughly equipped for his work ; and it does not make any difference whether he is a Canadian or an Englishman, or an Australian, so long as he is a British subject. I understand that a number of the professors in the military college are Canadians.

We have done it in some cases, I admit, to assist a college newspaper, and in that way we have attracted the attention of students in the other colonies. But I have no objection to accepting the hon. gentleman's suggestion, and perhaps it will help me in resisting applications, because it has taken a good deal of my time, I confess, to keep this item down to the point at which it i3 now.
The hon. gentleman's explanation does not satisfy me. He seems to think that because an expenditure is the same as it was last year it must be all right. I do not think that is any reason at all.

I merely stated the fact casually. My hon. friend can draw any conclusion he likes. Now I will finish the list. Transport and travelling expenses, $2,000-if my hon. friend will permit me to say it, the same as last year.
Transport for what?
To pay the expenses of the cadets to and fro when they return home. We also pay the travelling expenses of the professors when they are on duty.
What travelling do they do?

They sometimes go to Montreal and Toronto to attend meetings of the universities, meetings where engineering and scientific matters are dealt with. Sometimes the commandant or a professor might want to visit West Point academy; sometimes they are called here on business connected with the college, to confer with the department. There are twelve professors.
Mi-. FOWLER. Have they all occasion to travel?
The principal part of this expenditure is for the cadets.
I find that the amount paid last year for the travelling expenses of the cadets was $029; so that the larger amount is not for the cadets.
What are the tuition fees ?
$100 a year.

You charge a student a tuition fee of $100 a year, and under those circumstances I cannot see how it is that you pay his travelling expenses. It does seem to be an anomaly. I could understand if you give him free tuition that you might carry him to college and take him back home again ; but when you charge him a tuition fee, why should you pay his travelling expenses ?
I suppose it is no answer to say so. but we are simply continuing the conditions which have existed for thirty years.
Does it not seem rather absurd ?
I confess that I have not looked into it personally.
I know some cadets who have gone to the college and returned home again whose expenses were paid by-themselves.
They are all treated alike. There is a regulation.
How many cadets are there ?
About 95.
Do you pay the travelling expenses of each to yud from his home ?
So I am informed.
I think there must be something wrong about that. I think the travelling expenses must be paid when the cadets are taken away somewhere. How many times a year do you transport them to and fro ?
Once.
You bring them to the college and send them home ?
Send them home.
One trip ?
Yes.

If you pay the expenses of one trip, I do not see how it is that you do not pay the cadet for his holidays as well. I think you had better get the Militia Council at this college, and see if they cannot wipe out a few of these anomalies.
At what page of the Auditor General's Report does that appear ?
Q-91. There were only travelling expenses paid for fourteen cadets last year.

Those were the graduates. I quote from the Royal Alili-tary College regulations, regulation No. 22 :
An allowance for travelling expenses at the rate of four cents a mile for the number of miles beyond 500 necessarily travelled between the headquarters of the military district in which he resides and the college will be paid to each cadet at the time he is first admitted, and a similar allowance for travelling expenses to the headquarters of the same military district will be paid to each cadet who has completed the full period of the college and obtained a certificate of good conduct. No allowance for travelling expenses will be granted to those who reside less than 500 miles from the college.
That seems a reasonable and proper provision.
That Is not the same proposition that was explained to us a moment ago.

The object is to put a man living in British Columbia, or in some other distant portion of tlie country, on the same footing as tlie man living in Montreal.
Mr. FOWLER, That is an altogether different thing. It was equalizing the difference between distant and near points.
Does this mean bringing a cadet to the college and paying all his expenses back home after his course is over ?
That is only at the beginning and the end. In addition to that. I am reminded that the expenses of the professors are paid to and from this country, and my hon. friend will see that is quite an item.
That will scarcely account for this large amount. Lou are not changing professors every year.
One or two change every year. They do not all go out at once. There is one going out this year and another going out next year, and so on.
Although this is a standing vote, it may not all be spent in one year ?

It may not all be spent in the year. In the coming year I think that three are going out. The expenses of cadets attending annual camp are paid, and sometimes cadets are sent out to do work for the college. They go to McGiil University annually to compete with some of the students there, and we pay their expenses. Every dollar of this expenditure is accounted for and is scanned by the Auditor General.
Has it always been like that ?

It has been the same from the beginning. My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson)'wants some more information, and I want to satisfy him in regard to the vote for equitation. That is a new charge. It only began last year, when a special vote of $5,000 was taken. That is for teaching young men to ride. The reason for this vote being taken is this : Formerly the horses of the artillery were used, but it was found very inconvenient to interfere with the artillery operations,- and it was decided that it would be very much better to construct stables and let the college own its own horses, I think myself it is a very much better regulation.
How many horses have been provided ?
Eight.
Has the department bought horses, or are they rented ?
This is only a provision made this year. Horses will be bought. As a matter of fact, thev have not yet been bought.

I do not want the hon. minister, on that advertising business, to take laurels to himself that are not altogether warranted. I notice by the pay-Mr. FOWLER.
ments that no Conservative publications have been favoured.
Last year must have been an off-year.
I think that is likely a sample of most of the years. The Book Lovers' Library gets $00.
That is not it.

That is for the purpose of getting very valuable and ready, up-to-date books for the students. I have no objection to that at all, because it is really an advantage to have them get a circulating library. The 'Canadian Mining Review'-
That is not a Liberal paper.

That is for the pure purpose of science, I suppose, $3 ; Halifax ' Chronicle.' which, I think, is pretty well determined in its politics, gets $50. The Montreal ' Herald -well, there may be some doubt about the (Montreal ' Herald,' but I have no doubt that $50 will fix it all right. Then there is the Ottawa ' Dane-brog.' $30 : that is a concession to outside neighbours, and no doubt that brings many a student to the college who would not otherwise find his way there. The ' Free Press ' may be a semi-independent paper, but it does not often show it. The ' Parliamentary Guide ' is, of course, not in politics, although the particular gentleman who provides it has some very strong ideas of political life, $50. The ' Rideau Press ' gets $200. What is the ' Rideau Press ' ? That seems to be a special paper. That must have a very wide circulation. Why should the ' Rideau Press ' get $200 when a servant of so many years' standing and so faithful as the ' Free Press ' only gets $50 ?
I think that was an accumulation for several years. I had some doubt as to whether I should give authority to pay the bill and it was finally compromised. The advertisement has been withdrawn.
Was that cut down by the Military Council ?
I am responsible for that.
W'hat is the Rideau Press?
It is the paper called ' Events.'
Why should it appear in the Auditor General's Report under the pseudonym of the-'Rideau Press?'
I suppose .that is the form in which the bill was rendered.
The Quebec ' Daily Telegram ' has $10 added to the general $50,

and of course the bright rays that come from the ' Soieii ' entitles it to $80, or more than half better than the ' Free Press ' or the ' Herald.' Then there is the ' Military Gazette ; ' there might be something in that.
I do not think any one in charge of that has been friendly to me.

Then there is the good Toronto ' Globe.' I hope the minister will add a little to the ' Globe ' for this year. The peculiar service it has been performing of late ; the way it swallowed itself in order to convince the government that it is friendly to it, deserves at least an addition of $10 if the Military Council would only pass it. Then there is ' Saturday Night.' I am afraid there is no hope for ' Saturday Night.' ' Saturday Night ' has seen its last $50 from the Military Council, but I suppose the Toronto ' Star ' will continue to have its $50 ?
It is not too bad that.
No ; they all have a political complexion.
Oh, my, no.
Why should you advertise in the ' Parliamentary Guide ? ' I did not think any one reads that except members of parliament and their wives ?
It is to inform the members of parliament.

Surely the members of parliament know about the Royal Military College. This publication known as ' Events ' and appearing here under the alias of the 'Rideau Press' is the property of the same individual who edits the ' Parliamentary Companion, so that this gentleman got $250.
' Events ' is not published any more.
Is it dead ?
The payment ceases because the paper itself ceases.
The payment ceased last year.
Was the $200 a contribution for funeral expenses ?
No, the paper is still published I am told.
I don't think so.
It was published last week.

Has the Minister of Militia any information to give about the selection of a site in Montreal for a military school ? We hear a great many stories
on the street, but I would like to have something authoritative from the minister ?

I am very glad to hear the statement made by the Minister of Militia, and I trust the deputation from the city of Montreal -will wait on him as soon as possible, because I strongly favour the idea of having a military school and a permanent corps established in Montreal so

that the regiments in that city anti its vicinity may be afforded facilities of instruction. Would my hon. friend say what is the school he intends to have in Montreal when the question of site is decided ? How many men will be there, and what is going to be done there altogether ?

There will be a company of infantry to begin with. I think there will also be a company of garrison artillery, but of that I cannot speak positively at present. There will be a certain number of engineers, of course.
How many men altogether 1
Between 200 or 300 of a permanent force.
And the different officers of the battalions in that district will go there to train ?
Yes, whenever they require to do so.
So that there will be altogether probably 300 or 400 men ?
I would think so.
What will become of the infantry school in St. John ? I understand that' it will be devoted entirely to cavalry ?
Yes. At St. John there will be stationed permanent-1;, a squadron of cavalry-120 men and horses.

Under this item I would like the minister to provide me with some information in regard to the new rifle range which is being built at Sussex. For instance, who is the inspector of the rifle range, what are his qualifications for the post, what will his pay be, and how much time is he supposed to devote per day to the inspection? When the armoury was built at Sussex, the inspector of that work was a person who had no qualification whatever for the position. He was not a builder or contractor in either stone work or wood work, but a merchant tailor. I trust that the minister has taken the precaution in this particular ease to procure a man for the position who has some qualification for it, and therefore I would like him to say who is appointed?

I cannot remember the name, but it seems to me that the gentleman appointed is a lawyer, a prominent member of the militia, a very good rifle shot, and one who has devoted a good deal of time to that branch of the work. I may be wrong, but I will bring the information which my hon. friend wants.

The ipinister may be right as to the profession, but he is wrong as to the qualifications. He has evidently been misinformed. I would like him to say who recommended the gentleman. Was it the person who has the patronage of the county?

The officer of the department is supposed to have satisfied himself as to the fitness of the man before recommending him. However. I will look into this case and give my hon. friend all the information I can.

I would like also' to be informed as to the length of time the contract is supposed to occupy. The minister will remember that the building of the armoury took about four times as long as the contract provided for. The contract price was $4,000 and there was something like $1,900 paid for inspection.

That must have been done in the Public Works Department.
Mr. FOWLER, It was. I do not assume that the minister did that, but I want to warn him.
For manufacture of reserve ammunition at Dominion arsenal, $75,000.

I see that the $75,000 purchase 3,000,000 rounds of ammunition, making the charge 2i cents a round. How does that price compare with the price of ammunition of the same kind he has been in the habit of purchasing? Does the country make anything out of this manufacture, or is the price the same, or more, or less?

The only way in which we could arrive at correct information in regard to that wouid be by comparing tbe cost writb tbe price in England; because it would not be fair to compare this ammunition with ammunition made by tbe trade in Canada. This is a very different article. It is a special article made up to a certain strength, Very carefully prepared, with the greatest possible precaution. I am told that the cost is less than tbe English price, or certainly not more, and much less than tbe cost in tbe United States.
I think it was stated last session by tbe minister that be was going to have another of these cartridge factories established. Does he propose to provide for that in tbe estimates?

What I said last year was that I thought the time had arrived for the establishment of another cartridge factory, but I would favour the idea of its being constructed by the trade. I said that there were people in England who had been making inquiries, and that I felt disposed to consider a pro-

posal which I expected to get from them, provided tliev would agree to manufacture in Canada all the explosives which we would require for our own factory, and which they would use in their own. Negotiations have been proceeding, but they have not materialized very much. I hope that- within six months the matter will have reached a business point.
The idea is that they may come here and establish it?
Yes. at or near Ottawa.
I see that the total amount expended on this factory is nearly |225,000. How much ammunition does the minister get?
About nine million rounds. There will be a further vote of $05,000 in the supplementaries for next year. Nine years ago the amount manufactured was 1,500.000 rounds.
At how much increased .expense?

The cost is $25 a thousand rounds and it used to be $30. Working extra hours, the capacity to-day is easily twenty million rounds. We can actually manufacture twenty million rounds, but without any difficulty nine million rounds, working hours nine a day.
Are these sent to the stores in the different districts?
Yes.
Do you keep a reserve supply in the different districts all tin* time?

The largest reserve is in Quebec. It is not desirable to say too much about this, but I can assure iny hon. friend we are looking after that matter, and there is a proper reserve at every point where it is likely to be required.
At the time the scare was on about the Welland canal, there were no cartridges within fifty miles of the spot.
That was the old Snider-Enfield cartridge. I do not think that, will occur again.
Is this the Lee-Eufield ammunition?
Yes, the new Ross rifles take the same cartridge, number 303.
I understand that rifle is defective.

Experts who have examined the rifle, mark II, which is
an improvement on the first, say it is one of the best, if not the best, in the world. M e have added to mark II many improvements which have been the result of experience.
I am glad to hear that the government made a contract with Sir Charles Ross to manufacture another rifle to replace rifle number 1, which was defective.
That is scarcely a fair inference. The original rifle compared very favourably with the imperial service rifle, but since then changes have been made and we have a rifle which cannot be excelled.
What did you do with the rifles already made?

A thousand rifles were issued to the Mounted Police and 500 to the Marine and Fisheries Department, but none had been issued to the militia. The chief change is in the back sight so there is very little difficulty in placing the new sight upon the mark I rifle. I have a telegram saying that after the 1st July, rifles will be issued at the rate of from 100 to 150 a day.
I have seen some criticisms of that rifle.

There were very severe criticisms of the first rifle and those criticisms I submitted to Colonel Cotton. Colonel Cotton went himself to Quebec to institute a most searching investigation, and he says that in every case the criticism was not fair, and rifle mark two is free from all the defects mentioned in that criticism.
To promote dairying interests by advances for milk and cream, to be recouped out of the proceeds of sales of such butter and cheese, to be placed to the credit of the consolidated revenue fund, $40,000.

This stood over at the request of the hon. member for St. John who wanted an explanation of the method of dealing with those advances by the Agriculture Department. On looking up the item, I find that the amount of $1,000 in the public account has nothing to do with this vote. That is a special sum sent to my department by the Orange River Colony government to pay for some live stock purchased in Canada to be sent to South Africa. The item happened to be, at the end of the fiscal year, in the hands of the government, and thus appeared in the public accounts. With regard to the $10,000 all tills money is available on a special credit given by the Auditor General. The account is kept quite distinct from the ordinary business of the branch.

When revenue from the sale of butter is received, it is deposited to the credit of the vote of $40,000. For every dollar which is paid out of this vote, an equal sum must be, and is, returned to it. The amount may be expended two or three times over in the season. There is a statement in regard to this in the Auditor General's Report, page H-101 governing credit and debit account. It will be seen here that although the vote was only $40,000, the expenditure was $126,062,43-that is, the amount was paid out nearly three times over. The revenue was $156,320.76. This apparently extraordinary condition is due to the fact that a large amount had been paid in on account of sales of butter. The account runs for the season and not for the fiscal year, and the balance as on 1st July appears in the Auditor General's Report." But that balance will be entirely misleading as regards the season, because it appears right in the middle of the season for which the money is used by the department. But, of course, the statement of the account has to close at the end of the fiscal year. The revenue credited to this account does not appear in the public accounts, because the money is never actually expended, and the vote itself is not shown as an expenditure against the Agricultural Department in the public accounts. Page 33 of part 3, Public Accounts ending 30th June, 1004, shows the total expenditure for the Commissioner's Branch, Agriculture and Dairying, to be $219,993.70. This is the expenditure of the vote of $220,-
000.	There is no item in the public accounts reports as to this $40,000 vote.
I believe this is a full explanation of what my hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) desired, and therefore I would ask the committee to pass the appropriation.

My attention was called to the statement in the Auditor General's Report and I have looked it over. The balance to the debit of the account amounts to $10.63 which has been placed to the credit of the department. But I notice a rather peculiar thing with regard to it, and that is that this is not a statement for one year or one season, but includes the summer season of 1902, the winter season of 1902-3, the summer season of 1903, the winter season of 1903-4 and the summer season of 1904. The revenue for the winter season of 1903-4 and the summer season of 1904 was $23,610 and the expenditure $20,420. And that would make a difference of $3,190 for one year.

The items of 1902 and
1902-3 appear because some of the payments for butter which had been sold in those seasons was not received until after July 1st, 1903. This is the explanation given me by the accountant.
Another reason for the increased revenue is that in the summer season of 1902 there appears a revenue from Innisfail of $1,167, and no expenditure.
- That is a case such as I explained-the receipt of money for butter sold in 1902, the money coming in after the end of that fiscal year.
What is this money used for ?

This is placed at the disposal of the department to make advances to the patrons of the creameries we run in the Northwest. The whole matter was explained last night, but I had not a full explanation in answer to the question of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel).
Does the minister propose to continue this work after the establishment of the new provinces ?
I think we will close up the work there within the next year or two.
And hand it over to the new provinces as was done in the case of the eastern provinces ?

Yes, as soon as they are able to take it over.
Some resolutions reported.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.

I beg to lay on the table a supplementary return to an order of the House dated 2Uth March last, relating to Thermograph records used in the transportation of perishable products in cold storage and the contracts entered into with steamship companies for installing cold storage. I may explain that I am not laying every contract on the table, but I am giving specimens of the contracts. The other contracts are exactly similar to those included in the return.
Ml1. BARKER. What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
To-morrow,
I expect the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will be here. We may take one or two minor Bills ; then go into Committee of Supply, taking up the estimates of the Departments of Trade and Commerce and Public Works.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.05 p.m.
